titleSource: The End of Time Management: Illusions and Italians

sittings.bodyEn: Forget filling every second, because busyness is usually a costume for avoiding the few important actions that feel uncomfortable. Calling weak leads, tidying a contact list, or walking papers around an office can look like a career and still change nothing. That costume will not get you out of the building or onto a trip, so it is useless for the life in the earlier chapters. More output from fewer actions is possible here, and the chapter says the cut is required. The work from here is elimination. Follow the instructions and the aim is about twice to six times the personal output, with income held or raised. What you do matters more than how quickly you finish a thing that should not be done.

terms.hook: Removing the work that does not move the goal, before you try to do the rest faster.

sittings.bodyEn: You already named what the time is for, and this chapter frees that time without giving up the income. An employee uses the gain as leverage for two things at once, higher pay and a remote arrangement. The usual order for this life is definition, then elimination, then automation, then liberation. Employees who mean to stay employees reverse the last two, because they need to get free of the office before a short week is safe. A room that expects motion from nine to five can punish a short schedule even when the results are higher, and the request becomes full hours plus several times the output. This chapter is meant to make an employee more costly to fire than to raise and release, and only then do the hours drop so the dreamline can use them. An owner uses the same tools to do less personal work while revenue rises, which sets up automation and then liberation.

terms.hook: For employees staying employed, leave the office culture before a short week, or the culture will demand the hours back.

sittings.bodyEn: Effectiveness is doing the things that move you toward your goals. Efficiency is finishing a chosen task with little waste, whether that task mattered or not. Efficient and ineffective is the default setting. A skilled door-to-door seller can be excellent at that method and still ineffective if a letter or an email would sell more. Checking mail dozens of times a day, with clever folders, can be efficient and still be wheel-spinning. Doing an unimportant thing well does not make it important. A task that consumes a long time is not important because it consumed a long time.

terms.hook: Choosing the tasks that move the goal.
Doing a task economically, after it has earned its place.

sittings.bodyEn: Pareto's law is used here as the 80/20 split: about eighty percent of outputs come from about twenty percent of inputs, and the split is often sharper. Ratios near ninety to ten, ninety-five to five, or ninety-nine to one show up often, and the minimum ratio to hunt is eighty to twenty. Set aside a day, ignore what feels urgent, and ask two questions of your work and your life. The first question asks which twenty percent of sources cause eighty percent of your problems and unhappiness. The second asks which twenty percent produce eighty percent of the outcomes and happiness you want. Apply both to friends, customers, advertising, and even how you rest, and expect the truth to sting. Find waste you can remove and strengths you can multiply, and treat a lack of time as a lack of priorities.

terms.hook: A rough split where a small share of inputs creates most of the results, and most of the trouble.
Hours spent because the day is supposed to look full, not because the work is needed.

sittings.bodyEn: In the chapter's company, five wholesale customers out of more than one hundred twenty brought about ninety-five percent of revenue and ordered without chasing, while almost all the hours and almost all the misery sat with the rest. The cut stopped contact with about ninety-five percent, fired two abusive accounts that were a small slice of profit and most of the anger, and kept the best few as the pattern to copy. One of those two stayed once the abuse was refused, similar buyers were added, and more customers were not treated as a goal. Monthly income went from about thirty thousand dollars to about sixty thousand in four weeks, and hours fell from over eighty to about fifteen. The same cut on ads, keeping the ones that made at least eighty percent of revenue, dropped advertising cost by more than seventy percent and nearly doubled direct sales in eight weeks. The same cut on partners, focusing on two affiliates who made about ninety percent and pausing hundreds of the rest, took management from several hours a week to about one hour a month and lifted that income by more than half. Most things make no difference, so being busy is lazy thinking, and in a new setting you may try widely for a month or two before you know what to keep.

The nine-to-five day is a shared habit, not a law of the work, and people fill whatever block they are given. Offer fifteen hours and the day will fill, and offer a sudden two-hour emergency and the deadline work often gets done anyway. Parkinson's law says a task swells in felt importance and complexity in proportion to the time allowed for it. A one-day deadline forces the essentials and often a better result, a week invites a mountain made from a small hill, and two months invites a monster. The two moves invert each other. One limits the tasks to the important so the day gets shorter, which is the 80/20 cut, and the other shortens the time so the tasks shrink to the important, which is Parkinson's law. Use both: name the few critical tasks that drive the income, put very short and clear deadlines on them, and treat a missing fence as permission for trivia to eat the day.

terms.hook: A task swells to fill the time you give it, so a short deadline keeps only the essential work.

sittings.bodyEn: The first cut is a medical one: after a heart attack you may work two hours a day for three months, and five, four, or three hours are not the exercise. Write what survives inside those two hours. Then run a second heart attack that leaves two hours in the whole week, and write what still survives. Next, drop four-fifths of the time sinks, including mail, calls, meetings, paperwork, customers, and offers, choosing the cuts that protect income. Name the three activities you use to feel busy while you postpone something uncomfortable. Use the four-fifths question about once a month so the list cannot grow back. The chapter treats this page as required, because simplicity here is a ruthless cut.

List the few people who create most of your enjoyment and momentum, and the few who create most of your anger and second-guessing. Move hours toward the first group, and ask what happens if you stop seeing the second, using a written fear page if you freeze. Also name the commitments, thoughts, and people that show up whenever you feel starved for time. Your days start to resemble the handful of people you see most, so a person who does not increase your strength is reducing it. Tell them the concern with tact: an attack confirms the cut, and a promise of change earns two weeks apart and then a trial with an end date and a pass-or-fail test. If that talk is too hot, be mid-task when they call and already booked when they invite you. The relief is what makes a full stop easier later, and poisonous company does not have a claim on your calendar.

One salesman in the chapter went from about forty hours to about eighteen, with Monday and Friday off and about four times the results, after five weeks of one repeating question. At least three times a day, at set times, ask whether you are being productive or merely active, which means whether you are inventing tasks to avoid the important one. Write tomorrow's list tonight on paper folded into a pocket, because a software list can grow without end, and allow two mission-critical items. If several items all feel crucial, ask of each whether the day would be enough if that item were the only finish. When something screams as urgent, ask what happens if you skip it and whether it deserves to delay the important work, and do not spend the last hour saving a five-dollar fee while the real task sits open. Do those two items one at a time from start to finish, because split attention invites more interruptions and weaker results. Put the question where you will see it at least three times a day, on a note or a chime, and let a tracker nag you when an avoidance site runs past a limit you set.

Use the short-deadline law on the calendar and on the single task. Try leaving around four, and try taking Monday or Friday off, so the remaining hours have to hold the real work and a life outside the job has room. If a boss watches every minute, later chapters handle the escape, and the shorter fence is still the aim. On the task, keep the list tiny and set a deadline short enough that trivia cannot swell, using a countdown you type into the browser if you need a clock. For two days, stop bouncing choices back to other people and propose the plan, at home and at work. A meal, a film, or a next step can be a suggestion or a trial you will replace if it fails. The lines can be as plain as offering a suggestion, proposing a plan, or naming a try that can be swapped.

The 80/20 questions choose the few inputs that create most of the results and most of the pain. Parkinson's law keeps those few inside a short deadline so trivia cannot swell. Doing every task faster, staying for eight hours out of habit, or multitasking the urgent queue undoes the chapter. Employees turn the extra output into pay and a remote agreement before they cut visible hours. Owners cut their own labor while revenue holds, which is the setup for later automation. Two critical items, finished one at a time, are the daily shape of both laws.
sittings.prompt: How do the 80/20 split and Parkinson's law work together here?
choices: Do every task faster, and keep the day at eight hours so nothing is missed
Identify the few critical tasks, then give them very short and clear deadlines
Multitask the urgent queue so the important work happens in the gaps
Add more customers and more hours until income feels safe
